body_markdown:
The culmination of a life’s work can be measured in many ways. It’s seen in a career path from one’s teenage years to retirement. Or in the appreciation of a growing family. Or countless other achievements, but today we’re zooming in on something specific: the money you’ve saved over the years by doing DIY repairs.


We aren’t suggesting you dig through your receipts or your memory banks for an extensive analysis. Instead, we posed this question to our readers to learn about the vehicles you’ve owned, the memories you made fixing them, and the approximate savings in cold, hard cash from all those efforts. Of course you did not disappoint, so let’s get right into your responses.


## Over A Million!


Unsplash/Nejc Soklic


**Chris S:** I’ve probably saved myself well over 1.2 million dollars during a lifetime stretching from when I was 15 working on my mom’s cars, till my 80’s, and still working on my stable of cars and about to begin restoring a ’57 Studebaker Golden Hawk.


In addition to a garage attached to a house that I designed and built myself, I also have a separate three-car garage with workspace. It has a home-built paint booth with laminar airflow that is heated or cooled. Cost $35K in materials and would cost at least 150K if contracted out. I’ve built at least six show cars and seven drivers over the years. I used to keep track of the hours on a couple of the show cars. The hours range between 1000 and 1500 hours each.


I do all my own work except for machining and balancing the engines. After my last disaster, I now send my automatic transmissions out to a professional, too.


## Something Big


Getty Images


**Dan:** What would be the dollar figure? Something big, I guess.


In the ’70s and early ’80s, I had no choice (no money) but to keep my ’73 ‘Cuda going through high school and college, so every job was done by me. And that car liked annual tailpipes.


After college, I suppose I had the money, but I hated paying a higher hourly rate than what I was making. So I did the work. What else was I supposed to do, watch TV and stare at the labor bill? So every oil change, brake job, muffler repair, tune-up, and cabin air filter was done at home. Some big-ticket items I did were a head gasket on an early ’80s Firebird V-6, rear shocks and brake lines in a 2003 GMC Denali, and muffler replacement on an early ’80s Subaru (supposedly you need to replace the whole system). And let’s not forget the emission tweaks, wiper blades, and light bulbs to get through annual inspection every year.


I imagine the labor savings on auto repair were huge, tens of thousands of dollars over the last 40 years. Working on cars, though, gives you confidence to attack other things. I have never paid for a leaky drain or faucet, sheetrock repairs, garage door opener and springs, three kitchen remodels …


The number keeps growing. And now my daughters use Google to help them figure out home and auto repairs because they saw what was possible. And the number will grow for a long time into the future.


**Clare S:** Impossible to estimate, since I have only paid for paint, machine work, and a few emergency on-road repairs in 58 years of driving—doing all the labour on my vehicles—usually owning two at a time, and numbering in the thirties—from 1928 on up, American, Japanese, English, and European—all but one purchased used and often abused. Likely in the hundreds of thousands!


**Steve H:** I have no idea how much I have saved, but it would be a lot since I am old. In college, my ’67 Cougar was hit several times, and I used the insurance money to pay for school and just bought another can of Bondo each time. So my car paid for some of my degree, so that’s a big payback over my career as an engineer.


I’ve never had a new car, and now I don’t want one, but keeping cars a long time without significant repair costs saves both car payments and the higher insurance that a newer car costs.


I can afford to have my wife not work, feed six kids, and still drive a fast convertible due to my skills learned and work done over the years. I think that I am well ahead of the game, and I’m not helpless when there is trouble with my or a friend’s car.


**DUB6:** Like you, Sajeev, I’m not even going to attempt to go back and do that math for 60+ years of DIY stuff vs. hiring it all done. But I did do a little simple calculating based on some things I and some family members had done over the last few years at shops. Unlike you, I didn’t find that parts prices were the biggest percentage—instead, it was labor charges.


Obviously, the price of parts is a big variable in shop prices—oil and filters are much cheaper than transmission rebuild kits—but I did take a pretty broad sampling of different types of work. The average labor charges in the work I looked at were almost 70% of the total—and when the “incidentals” were added (shop supplies, mostly), it was plain to me that nearly 3/4 of shop work prices isn’t for parts. Now, yes, I agree that my own labor isn’t (or shouldn’t be) considered free, but in my wildest dreams I never collected $87.50 an hour for basic wrenching activities!


For a shop-rated 7.5 hours, the actual labor charge was $656.25 of an $875 total bill (including parts, labor, misc, and before sales tax). If I had done the DIY work and paid myself $30 per hour, even if I took TEN hours to do it (kind of my rough estimate), I would have saved approx. $350 +/- if all else was equal (i.e., parts costs). Like you, I will also shop around on parts, whereas the pro shops often don’t take the time. Plus, I don’t charge myself for shop rags and hand-cleaning supplies, but some shops do—and more. Frankly, I’m not even gonna declare that I’m worth thirty bucks an hour, but one has to plug something into the equation!


So, even though I’m working with some relatively soupy examples here, I estimate that my DIY work has saved me around 40% in labor alone over the course of the years. All in all, I’m willing to project that on an overall basis (averaging out over more AND less expensive jobs), I’ve saved close to 50% working in my own garage shop. Fifty percent of what amount? Heck, I dunno—less than infinity and more than zero!


**Tinkerah:** Incalculable. Been fixing my and my family’s cars since 1978. Now add on all the hot-rodding and fabricating that is hard to farm out at any price. Then multiply by all the jobs that would’ve been botched by hourly shops and had to have been corrected or done over…It would’ve soured me on the entire hobby.


**Andy:** Having done so many complete restorations since 1970, it is impossible to compute how much I saved, not to mention all my friends’ cars I have worked on for free. However, we purchase new Nissan models every few years and let them do the service, which only amounts to $300 a year. This ensures we are covered for a minimal amount of getting ripped off for their service. One, my own fault, was for an inspection where I was charged $100 for wiper blades that only lasted six months!


## To The Contrary


Rob Siegel


**Desmond G:** Over the decades, probably a few thousand dollars. Some of my savings were negated by jobs I tried but couldn’t do properly—or at least to the standard I had hoped for.


However, what I’ve saved by paying someone else to do the wrenching is worth vastly more than that. Countless hours of being frustrated beyond the point of absolute fury; thousands of cuts, scrapes, bruises, busted knuckles, and sore joints; hundreds of various automotive fluid stains; my ability to appreciate cars at all; and even my cars themselves.


Because if I had to do all of the work on my own cars, I have few doubts that I eventually would have gotten so angry that I ended up beating at least one of them into scrap metal with a sledgehammer by now. I can’t even begin to convey how irrationally livid I usually become when having to fix a car.


**Keith E:** Learning how to DIY opened the door to project cars and restorations… not so sure the end result has been savings!


## It isn’t about the money?


[Stefan Lombard](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/stefan-lombard/)


**Binksman:** My family lives the life it does because of me being able to do my own work on vehicles, or the house, or the property. While I’ve never itemized its value, it is apparent enough that I am making sure to pass that knowledge and skills to my kids. They will probably never inherit anything from me, but I can give them that.


The problem with being able to do those things is that I rarely “save” money because it frees up money to do other things. I repair my vehicles and can thus afford to buy old motorcycles, which of course need repair. And so on…


**JP:** Been repairing my cars since high school. I’m sure it has saved on the order of tens of thousands. As others have alluded to, there are indirect benefits as well. I’m getting to an age where I have a little more money and less free time. So I’ve started doing the time vs money calculation more often. But it’s hard to do that calculation well if you haven’t done a lot of work yourself first.


If I get a coupon for a $20 oil change, I jump on it. But if I get an $800 labor charge for something I can do in an hour, I will DIY. But again, I am only able to make those decisions well because I have spent the time and gotten the busted knuckles to know what it’s all worth.


**John B:** Yes, it is often out of necessity. Many years ago, I learned how to rebuild carburetors because I could not trust a repair shop to do it correctly. I don’t know about money saved, although it would be interesting to figure it out.


**John D:** Being able to do my own maintenance and save money in the process has enabled me to drive an old car longer economically. My primary vehicle is 23 years old with 320,000 miles and still going strong. That was never my plan, but keeping it running is just too convenient and inexpensive. The car won’t give me a reason to buy something new and shiny. I’d drive it cross-country right now.


**Jeff G:** There is another way of looking at this.


I have a 20-year-old BMW E60 530i. The only way it is economical to keep one of those for 20 years is if I am only paying for parts. (Which, to be fair, aren’t particularly high.) That car was $60K new. The average person keeps a new car just under nine years, because they start getting hammered by repair labor costs.


So if I was the average person, I would have eaten at least $100K in depreciation costs, as opposed to $57K (Kelly Blue Book estimate for excellent condition and 162,000 miles) keeping the car this long. Keeping in mind I don’t take the depreciation hit until I get rid of the car.


And that is before getting to avoided labor. For example, I have replaced the valve cover, oil pan, and oil filter manifold gaskets (Lord only knows why BMW can’t keep oil in an otherwise outstanding engine). That alone is a $4500 labor bill. Add on refurbishing and periodic maintenance labor costs, and I have saved at least another $50k on that car alone. Take away the cost of tools (guessing around $20K accumulated over 40 years), and I’m still waaaay ahead of the game. Also, it is absolutely true that the more you know how to do, the more you know how to do more.


## Time Vs. Money


Rolls-Royce


**Tim:** I don’t do everything on my own, but I do most things. I use a “time vs. money” approach, cross-applied to my ability to perform the maintenance or solve the problem myself. That means I do lots of easy things like replace brake pads, rotors, coils, failed sensors, batteries, etc. Going back far enough, it could have included an alternator, radiator, etc., but I haven’t had one of those fail in decades.


On my newer vehicles, I no longer change the oil. My local dealer runs a loss leader on doing an oil change, tire rotation, multi-point inspection, and fluid top-off. The obvious goal is to find any maintenance issues that need to be addressed and have the customer opt to have the service performed while the vehicle is conveniently at the shop. But nothing has ever arisen other than a recommended air filter or cabin air filter change, which I can do myself. Adding that the dealer picks up the vehicle and drops it off, I’m not even out time waiting at the service center. Not only is the cost of the service less than I would pay for oil and a filter, adding my time to make a trip to the store to buy the oil and filter, then to drop off the used oil, not even counting the time to do the oil change and tire rotation, but I could never hope to break even with DIY.
